video.title: Shoulder Adduction Unlocks the Tennis Forehand

classification.reason: The coach explains the mechanics of shoulder adduction as the final link in the forehand kinetic chain, how to set up the contact zone, and how to probe the ball for clean contact.

problem.title_as_question: How should shoulder adduction be used to unlock a consistent forehand contact zone?
problem.definition: Shoulder adduction naturally pulls across the body and turns the racket face downward; without positioning the body so this motion drives back-to-front with a stable string angle, players miss sideways, net the ball, or frame shots.
prerequisites: Ability to sustain slow rallies or feed balls
problem.target_player: 2.5 to 4.5 players who want to stop missing and framing forehands and achieve clean consistency

symptoms.description: The racket turns completely over, causing the ball to be hit sideways and downward into the court or net.
The ball is shanked or framed off the outside of the racket frame.
The racket face closes excessively, rotating approximately 100 degrees through the contact zone instead of staying relatively stable.
The hitting elbow remains stuck behind the plane of the hips during the forward swing.

causes.statement: Shoulder adduction naturally pulls the arm across the body and induces internal shoulder rotation, which sends the ball sideways and down if unguided.
The hitting elbow does not pass the plane of the hips, preventing shoulder adduction from directing the racket forward into the ball.
The player fails to probe and position the body properly relative to the ball, forcing contact outside the optimal back-to-front adduction zone.
The player focuses on uncoiling the torso and generating excessive velocity before mastering clean contact with the arm's final adduction link.

angles.summary: Shoulder adduction pulls across the body and naturally couples with internal shoulder rotation, which must be oriented back-to-front within a specific contact zone.
Refutes the idea of violently rolling the racket over the ball, explaining that the string angle should only change about 10 degrees through contact rather than 100 degrees.
Develop the internal sensation of moving through contact with a consistent, slightly downward string angle powered by a pull across the chest.
Demonstrates how low, high, too far, and too close balls require body tilt or altered finish heights to preserve the required shoulder adduction motion.
Observes that tour professionals on bad bounces will adjust their swing path into a hook or flick to maintain necessary shoulder adduction even when out of position.

solutions.summary: Swing forward until the hitting elbow clearly passes the plane of the hips before releasing shoulder adduction.
Check the string angle through the contact zone to ensure it changes only about 10 degrees on a slight downward angle rather than closing 100 degrees over the ball.
solutions.external_goal: Keep the string face angle changing by no more than roughly 10 degrees through contact

ban_conflict.note: Actively turning the racket over the ball during contact causes severe timing errors and mishits.

solutions.summary: Rally slowly using only the shoulder adduction arm motion while ignoring torso uncoiling and hip drive to master clean ball contact.
solutions.external_goal: Hit slow rally balls cleanly over the net using only the arm motion

solutions.summary: Adjust your body position and hip tilt to probe the ball into the precise front window where shoulder adduction drives cleanly back-to-front.
solutions.external_goal: Position the body so the ball arrives within the front contact window
